title: This $100 Box Can See Invisible Particles From Space!
summary:
Right now, tiny invisible particles are zooming through your body. You can't see them, feel them, or hear them. They're called muons, and they come from space. Scientists have built a small device that can detect them—and it costs only $100!

The device is called CosmicWatch. It's about the size of a box of animal crackers. When a muon passes through it, the device flashes and counts it. You can later download the data and study it. "CosmicWatch detectors allow us to do far more physics at a dramatically lower cost," said Spencer Axani, a physics professor at the University of Delaware who created it.

Muons are created when cosmic rays—extremely energetic particles from exploding stars—hit atoms high in Earth's atmosphere. These collisions create showers of secondary particles, including muons. Muons can travel through the atmosphere and even deep underground. They can pass through walls, rock, and even people without causing any harm.

Scientists use muons to study powerful events in space, like supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. In 2016, muon technology helped discover a hidden corridor inside the Great Pyramid of Giza! That's like using invisible particles to X-ray a pyramid.

Before CosmicWatch, muon detectors were big and expensive. "A typical undergraduate physics lab course uses a rack of electronics about the size of a small bookshelf to measure muons," Axani said. Now, high school students can do it too.

Axani first built CosmicWatch in 2017 when he was a student at MIT. He wanted a small detector for the IceCube observatory in Antarctica. Then he realized it could help students learn about physics. He recently released the third version, which can monitor its surroundings and gather data faster.

So next time you feel a tiny tickle, it's not a muon—but they're there, passing through you right now!
why_it_matters: Knowing that invisible particles are passing through you right now makes science feel real, and cheap tools like this mean your own school could do the same experiments.

background_read: Muons were discovered in the 1930s by scientists who were studying cosmic rays from space — they were surprised to find these tiny particles raining down on Earth.
The IceCube observatory (a huge detector buried deep in the ice at the South Pole) studies particles from space, and that is where Spencer Axani first wanted to use a small detector.
MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a famous science university in the United States) is where Axani built the first CosmicWatch.
Article_Structure: WHO: Spencer Axani, a physics professor at the University of Delaware who built CosmicWatch, and the student labs and scientists who now use it.
WHAT: A $100 box-sized detector that flashes and counts muons passing through it, and can save the data for study.
WHERE: Muons are made high in Earth's atmosphere; the detectors are used in classrooms and labs, and muons helped find a hidden corridor in the Great Pyramid of Giza.
WHY: It lets students do real physics for very little money, instead of needing a rack of electronics the size of a bookshelf.

perspectives.description: They love it because real particle physics is now possible for the price of a toy, not a whole lab.
Some may point out that a very cheap detector is less precise than big lab machines, so its results need checking.
Muon detectors already solved a real mystery by finding a hidden corridor inside the Great Pyramid of Giza.
